newsitem.title: CHINA: China zinc firms seen forced to cover in market.
newsitem.headline: China zinc firms seen forced to cover in market.

text.p: Zinc spells danger for Chinese producers, who could be forced to fork out huge sums to cover short positions after selling forward when the price was $400 a tonne lower than it is today, traders said on Thursday.

Industry sources close to the Chinese government have told Reuters they believe Chinese zinc producers were the victims of an orchestrated market squeeze, which has been successful due to tight zinc supplies stemming from low stocks and strong demand.

Rumours have swirled for months that China's zinc producers, principally the Zhuzhou smelter which makes Torch brand metal, sold huge forward contracts at prices ranging from $1,100 to $1,350 a tonne at the end of last year.
With the contracts now falling due, the Chinese may have to buy metal at much higher current prices on the open market to meet their obligations.
The London Metal Exchange (LME) official price for cash zinc was quoted at $1,570/$1,571 at the market's close on Wednesday.
"Zinc is a dangerous game at the moment," a Chinese metal trader said.
Chinese producers and their trading representatives have long denied the rumours that they locked in massive zinc sales at low prices.

But a recent report in a publication associated with Beijing's metals production arm China National Nonferrous Metals Corp (CNNC) said a decision was made late in 1996 that $1,100 would be a good level at which to establish short positions.
"When that price level was reached, Chinese hedge selling of zinc apparently increased," the publication, China Metals, said.
"As zinc prices further climbed, some Chinese traders, Zhuzhou smelter in particular, went beyond hedging and established considerable short positions," it said.
The report said Zhuzhou short-sold 90,000 tonnes of zinc in three months on the LME.
"Unconfirmed reports say that total Chinese forward selling has amounted to 250,000 tonnes," China Metals said.
Calculating the difference between current LME zinc prices and levels prevailing at the end of 1996, the loss on 250,000 tonnes of the metal would now be over $100 million.
The Chinese smelters have been working overtime all year to churn out metal to take advantage of the rising zinc prices.
Official media have reported that China's zinc output in the first five months of 1997 was up 35 percent on the same year-ago period, at 537,000 tonnes.
In the same five months, exports were up 128 percent at 191,200 tonnes compared with the first five months of 1996, the reports said.

The Chinese are locked in a battle with Swiss trading house Glencore which is believed by London dealers to have a large long position in zinc and which recently approached the LME with queries about the quality of Torch zinc, dealers said.

The queries about a small lot of Torch metal, which Glencore said were made on behalf of a customer, led to an order from the LME for random sampling of all Torch metal in LME warehouses, which a source close to the matter said totalled around 30,000 tonnes.
Subsequent tests, the results of which have been seen by Reuters, showed the Torch zinc surpassed LME quality requirements.
"China has exported hundreds of thousands of tonnes of metal in recent years, and never has there been any problem," a state trading source said.
